JSON: Name: ecosystem_osh_trial Title: Cluster-randomized evaluation of an ecosystem-based design method for sustaining occupational safety and health interventions Short Hypothesis: Firms that implement an OSH intervention designed with an explicit ecosystem approach (actor alignment, integrated data/material flows, circular activities/strategies, and formal post-implementation governance) will exhibit a greater reduction in workplace injury incidence rate at 12 months post-implementation than firms that implement a standard PDCA-based OSH intervention. Related Work: Existing approaches to OSH intervention design emphasize iterative management cycles (PDCA), participatory methods, and theory-driven realist evaluations. Prior work has documented that participatory co-creation and iterative improvement increase short-term uptake and acceptability, while realist analyses identify contextual mechanisms that affect outcomes. Limitations of current methods include: (1) scarce systematic integration of multi-actor governance and formalized post-implementation processes, (2) weak attention to continuous data/material flow management and cross-organizational value capture, (3) predominance of qualitative or non-randomized designs that limit causal inference about long-term effectiveness, and (4) lack of component-level (ablation) evidence quantifying which design elements drive sustained impact. No established empirical pipeline rigorously compares a multi-element ecosystem design against standard PDCA or isolates the marginal contribution of governance, actor alignment, and data integration. Abstract: This study evaluates whether an ecosystem-based design for occupational safety and health (OSH) interventions produces larger and more sustained reductions in workplace injuries than standard PDCA-based designs. The ecosystem design operationalizes five elements—value articulation, actor selection and alignment, integrated data/material flows, circular activities and strategies, and formal governance including post-implementation monitoring. We will conduct a cluster-randomized trial across firms stratified by sector and size, comparing the ecosystem-designed intervention to a PDCA control and a participatory control. Primary outcome is injury incidence per 100 full-time equivalents at 12 months; secondary outcomes include safety climate, near-miss reporting rates, intervention continuation, and cost per avoided injury. The main contribution is a causal test of an ecosystem design and an internal ablation study to quantify the marginal effects of governance and data-integration components. Expected outcome: quantification of whether and which ecosystem elements increase long-term OSH effectiveness and practical guidance for scaling sustainable interventions. Experiments: Design: cluster-randomized controlled trial with three arms (ecosystem intervention, PDCA control, participatory control) and embedded ablation within the ecosystem arm. Sampling: recruit 180 firms across three countries (60 per arm), stratified by sector (manufacturing, construction, ports/fishing) and size (SME vs larger); mean cluster workforce = 50 FTE. Pre-intervention period: collect 12 months baseline data. Randomization: at firm level with blocking by country and size. Datasets: firm injury logs (OSHA-equivalent), near-miss reports, HR exposure hours, safety climate survey (standardized Likert instrument), system logs from any data-sharing platforms, intervention cost records. Baselines: PDCA implementation protocol; participatory-only implementation (worker workshops + training). Ablation: randomly assign half of ecosystem-arm firms to remove (A) post-implementation governance (no formal monitoring body) and half to remove (B) integrated data/materials flow tools (no shared platform), enabling three sub-arms (full ecosystem, ecosystem minus governance, ecosystem minus data). Primary metric: change in injury incidence rate per 100 FTE at 12 months (count). Secondary metrics: change in safety climate score, near-miss reporting rate per 100 FTE, binary intervention continuation at 12 months, cost per avoided injury. Analysis: mixed-effects Poisson regression for injury counts with firm random effects and fixed effects for arm, time, covariates (sector, size); difference-in-differences estimate for pre/post; survival analysis (Cox) for continuation; per-protocol and intention-to-treat analyses. Power: detect 20% relative reduction in injury rate with alpha=0.05, power=0.8, ICC=0.05 yields ~60 clusters/arm given mean cluster size 50. Sensitivity: subgroup analyses by sector and firm size; pre-registered statistical analysis plan and multiple-testing correction. Data quality checks: audit sample of reported injuries against administrative records. Risk Factors and Limitations: Randomization constraints and ethical/practical refusal by firms may induce selection bias or contamination between arms. Underreporting and differential reporting incentives will bias injury and near-miss measures. Heterogeneity across sectors and countries limits external validity; observed effects may not generalize to untested sectors. External shocks (pandemics, regulatory changes, economic crises) can confound outcome attribution. ICC or smaller-than-expected effect sizes reduce statistical power; recruitment shortfalls can invalidate planned inference. Implementation fidelity variability across firms will create measurement noise; distinguishing design effects from delivery quality is challenging. Ablation sub-randomization reduces power for component estimates. Data integration platform dependence raises operational failure modes (downtime, access issues) producing missing data. Cost and human-resource requirements for ecosystem implementation may limit scalability to resource-constrained firms. Legal and privacy constraints may restrict sharing of administrative data across actors.
